strengths: Novel application of compressed sensing to attention head localization, achieving up to 50x fewer model evaluations than greedy baselines while maintaining comparable task-degradation efficacy (Table 4).

Broad empirical validation across 5 models spanning two model families (Llama, Qwen) and scales (1B-8B), and across 4 distinct capabilities (math, code, swearing, rhyming), lending some generality to the localization claims.

The generalization experiment (Table 3), showing heads identified on one dataset (e.g., GSM8K) transfer to degrade performance on a related dataset (Arithmetic), strengthens the claim that identified heads capture a genuine underlying capability rather than dataset-specific artifacts.
The discovery of 'universal heads' and scale-dependent localization (WMDP experiments) are interesting secondary findings that add nuance and open directions for future mechanistic work.
Clear problem formulation and algorithmic description (Section 3-4), with an ablation comparing Bernoulli vs. stratified sampling and different baselines, aiding reproducibility of the core method.
weaknesses: The additivity/linearity assumption underlying the compressed sensing formulation is only informally justified ('we assume...'); no direct empirical test comparing predicted additive effects vs. actual joint-ablation performance is presented to validate the core theoretical premise.

Head identification and hyperparameter selection (number of masks, sparsity) are both tuned per-task/per-model using the same 100-sample subset used to score candidate head sets, which risks overfitting the selection procedure to this exact subset; while final evaluation uses full datasets, the identification and hyperparameter tuning are not clearly separated from validation in a way that rules out subtle leakage or cherry-picking of hyperparameters per condition, which could bias comparisons against baselines that may not receive equivalent tuning effort.

Custom evaluation datasets for 'swearing' and 'rhyming' are minimally described (only 12 swearing prompts; rhyme dataset construction is vague and partly 'AI-assisted'), and profanity scoring via simple word-list matching is a coarse proxy for the intended capability, raising concerns about the reliability and reproducibility of two of the four core capability results.

No variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run analysis is reported for any of the main results (Tables 2-5), making it difficult to assess whether reported degradations (e.g., -1.1 vs -2.3 in Gen columns) reflect real differences or noise, especially given small identification-time sample sizes.

The choice of exactly top-5 heads as the standard unit of analysis across all models/tasks is only loosely justified by a single plateau plot for math (Figure 2) on one model; it is unclear whether this fixed k is appropriate across the very different scales and head counts (512-1024) of the studied models.

The 'universal heads' phenomenon is reported only for Llama models and not observed in Qwen models, but this asymmetry is not explained or investigated, leaving an unresolved gap in the generality of this secondary claim.

Scale-dependence conclusions (Section 6.2) rest on only three models and a single benchmark family (WMDP/MMLU), which is a fairly thin evidentiary base for the strong claim that 'task-specific heads for specific knowledge may emerge only at larger scales.'

Minor but notable presentation issues suggest incomplete proofreading (e.g., Table 1 lists 'Qwen 2.5 3B and Qwen 2.5 3B' instead of 7B and 3B; the code repository link in the abstract is left blank), which slightly undermines confidence in reproducibility artifacts.

The paper does not compare against other established interpretability/localization baselines beyond internally-defined greedy search (e.g., gradient-based attribution, activation patching), limiting the ability to contextualize how much of the observed localization is a general property versus an artifact of the ablation-based measurement approach itself.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, well-motivated method for localizing task-specific attention heads using compressed sensing, grounded in a plausible sparsity + approximate linearity assumption, and connects nicely to compressed sensing theory (O(k log(N/k)) measurements).

Extensive empirical validation across 6 models (Llama and Qwen, 1B-14B) and 4 diverse capabilities (math, code, swearing, rhyming), with consistent findings that ablating ~5 heads produces large task-specific degradation while sparing general capabilities (Table 2).

Good ablation/ generalization checks: cross-dataset validation (GSM8K heads affect Arithmetic and vice versa; MBPP heads affect HumanEval), comparison against greedy/one-shot-greedy baselines and ProxySPEX showing large efficiency gains (up to 50x fewer evaluations) with comparable accuracy, random-head and mean-vs-zero ablation controls.

Interesting secondary findings (universal heads, scale-dependent localization, GQA head clustering, WMDP/MMLU shared format heads) that enrich the paper's contribution and open directions for future mechanistic study.

Reasonably strong connection to prior mechanistic interpretability findings (e.g., independently recovering L16H21/L15H13 identified by Nikankin et al. for arithmetic), lending some external validity to the method.
Detailed appendix with hyperparameter search procedures, full head lists, and additional ablations, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The additivity/first-order linearity assumption underlying the Lasso-based recovery is asserted rather than rigorously validated; the paper acknowledges nonlinearity but provides only indirect empirical support (i.e., that recovery works) rather than a direct test of how well the linear model fits actual joint-ablation effects.

The claimed formal compressed-sensing guarantees (M ≈ O(k log(N/k))) are invoked loosely ("informally motivates") without an accompanying restricted isometry property (RIP)-style justification for the specific binary/stratified measurement matrices used, weakening the theoretical rigor implied by the title/framing.

Recall@k results (Table 7) are quite low (0.2-0.53) even at 300 evaluations, indicating the method's agreement with greedy "ground truth" is modest; the paper's explanation (noise, near-equal importance of extra heads) is plausible but not independently verified, leaving open how faithful the identified head sets truly are beyond the top 1-2 heads.

Task diversity is somewhat narrow and includes two custom, small, and seemingly ad hoc datasets (12 swearing prompts, ~113 rhyming pairs) without inter-rater/robustness analysis of the automatic scoring (e.g., profanity-word matching, CMU-dict rhyme checking), raising concerns about noise/label quality reflected in the very large error bars for SWEAR (e.g., ±30.2 for Qwen-14B) and RHYME.

The necessity-but-not-sufficiency finding (retaining only task heads yields poor performance) is only briefly mentioned in the intro as a 'preliminary experiment' without quantitative results, circuit analysis, or discussion of what this implies for the causal interpretation of 'task-specific' heads.

Hyperparameters (number of masks, sparsity level) are tuned per model/dataset via a small grid search using the actual evaluation task performance as the selection criterion (Appendix A.2), which could inflate reported efficiency numbers and reduces the method's plug-and-play practicality; the sensitivity of results to this tuning is not clearly quantified.

The scale-dependence and WMDP findings (Section 6.2) are based on a single model pair comparison (Llama 3.1 8B vs. 3.2 3B/1B) and speculative interpretation ("format-specific vs task-specific"), which is an interesting but underpowered claim given only 2-3 data points across scale.

The Impact Statement is minimal/boilerplate given that the paper explicitly discusses AI safety and model editing implications (including techniques that could disable/degrade specific capabilities), which merits more substantive discussion of dual-use risks (e.g., using localized heads to degrade safety-relevant behaviors).
